4.6.2 According to the EDHS 2024-25 June 2026 report, Tigray recorded higher infant and child mortality rates than the national average. The under-five mortality rate was 66 deaths per 1,000 live births in Tigray, compared with 51 nationally, while the infant mortality rate was 54 deaths per 1,000 live births compared with 39 nationally[footnote 88].

4.6.3 Regarding access to national health insurance, the same source noted:

‘Since 2011, Ethiopia has implemented the community-based health insurance (CBHI) scheme, aimed at reaching and covering the very large rural agricultural sector and small and informal sectors in urban settings. The overall objective of insurance coverage is to promote equitable access to sustainable, quality health care; increase financial protection; and enhance social inclusion for the majority of Ethiopian families via the health sector. The CBHI benefit package covers all outpatient and inpatient services at the health centre and hospital levels other than services related to dentures, eyeglasses, and cosmetic procedures (USAID 2019a).’[footnote 89]

4.6.4 The ESS EDHS 2024-25 June 2026 report noted that health insurance coverage in Tigray was substantially lower than the national average. While 45% of women and 51% of men nationally were covered by community-based or mutual health insurance schemes, only 10.6% of women and 7.9% of men in Tigray reported having any form of health insurance. Accordingly, 89.4% of women and 92.1% had no health insurance, compared with 54% of women and 49% of men nationally[footnote 90].

4.6.5 In August 2026 the Physicians for Human Rights (PHR), a non-governmental organisation that uses medical and scientific evidence to investigate and document alleged human rights violations[footnote 91], and the Organization for Justice and Accountability in the Horn of Africa (OJAH), an independent organisation that documents and preserves evidence relating to alleged human rights violations in the Horn of Africa[footnote 92] published a report on attacks on healthcare in Tigray, Amhara and Afar. According to the report Tigray’s health system remained affected by attacks on and damage to healthcare facilities and workers, alongside severe shortages of fuel, medicines and medical supplies, and financial restrictions. Citing the Tigray Regional Health Bureau, the report stated that fuel restrictions had affected ambulances, medical transport and vaccine cold-chain maintenance, while shortages of medicines and supplies had resulted in rationing and delayed procedures. Healthcare workers were also reported to have been without salaries since January 2026. The report stated that attacks on and damage to healthcare facilities, together with the loss of medicines, supplies and equipment, had impeded the ability of affected communities to access necessary healthcare[footnote 93].

4.6.6 On 28 September 2026, MSF reported that it suspended activities at Alamata Hospital due to the security situation following the resumption of fighting between TPLF-aligned and federal forces. According to MSF, staff were redeployed to support hospitals treating increasing numbers of war-wounded patients​[footnote 94].

4.7 Access to education

4.7.1 A June 2025 report by the Norwegian Refugee Council, a global humanitarian organisation helping people forced to flee[footnote 95] reported that 61 primary and 6 secondary schools operating before the conflict in Mai-Tsebri, Tselemti and Dima woredas had been damaged, looted or used as shelters. The NRC reported that more than 41,000 children were out of school and had no access to learning, nearly half of whom were girls[footnote 96].

4.7.2 A 23 September 2025 ACAPS report stated that, by September 2025, around 1.2 million children, approximately 46% of the school-age population, were out of school in Tigray, according to the regional Bureau of Education. The report attributed this primarily to the continuing social and economic impacts of the conflict[footnote 97].

4.7.3 The Global Education Cluster Dashboard updated September 2026 indicated that as of November 2025, 360 schools in Tigray were closed and 1.35 million children were out of school[footnote 98].

4.7.4 The Ethiopia Ministry of Education annual education statistics for 2025/25 provides data on gross national enrolment and net national enrolment rations at primary and secondary level nationally and regionally. GER measure indicates total enrolment at a given education level, regardless of age, as a percentage of the population of the official age group for that level at a level, all ages per population in the official age group as a percentage[footnote 99]. NER shows enrolment of children of the official age for that education level, as a percentage of the population in that same age group[footnote 100].

4.7.5 The table below, based on data from the Ethiopian Ministry of Education’s Annual Abstract for the 2024/25 academic year[footnote 101], compare school enrolment in Tigray with national enrolment rates:

1.1.4 According to an April 2026 article by Eurafrica Press & News, an online news and analysis platform reporting on political, economic and security issues in Africa and Europe[footnote 12], Tigray’s post-war economic recovery remained largely stalled three years after the Pretoria Agreement. The report cited business representatives as describing severe shortages of cash and finance, limited access to credit, fuel shortages and a lack of reconstruction, with much of the war-damaged industrial base remaining non-operational. It noted that factories which had previously been major employers and contributors to exports had not resumed normal operations. According to the report industry accounted for 26.3% of Tigray’s regional GDP in 2016/17, but that the sector’s contribution had fallen to an estimated 2% to 3% following the conflict due to destruction, displacement and stalled recovery. Business representatives interviewed by the report attributed continuing economic difficulties to both war-related damage and ongoing political instability, which they said had hindered economic recovery and investment[footnote 13].

1.2 Employment

1.2.1 The June 2026 Ethiopian Statistical Service (ESS) Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey (EDHS) report based on data collected between 1 August 2024 and 14 April 2025[footnote 14] (ESS EDHS 2024/25 June 2026 report) stated that 41% of women aged 15–49 and 87% of men were currently employed nationally. In Tigray 37.5% of women and 79.6% of men were employed[footnote 15].

1.2.2 The September 2026 Ethiopia Statistical Services (ESS) key findings report of the National Integrated Household Survey (ESS NIHS September 2026 report) stated the employment to population ratio in Tigray was 52.7%, compared with 61.3% nationally. Employment rates were lower for both men and women in Tigray than nationally, with 63.7% of men and 42.7% of women employed, compared with national rates of 71.8% and 50.9% respectively[footnote 16].

1.2.3 In terms of numbers, the same source indicated that in Tigray, 88.0% of the economically active population was employed, equivalent to 2,184,319 people out of 2,480,972 economically active individuals. Employment was concentrated in rural areas, where 1,561,862 people were employed, compared with 622,458 in urban areas. [The rural and urban employment figures sum to 2,184,320, one more than the source’s reported total of 2,184,319. Figures are reproduced as published]. Nationally, the employment rate among the economically active population was slightly higher at 90.4%, with 49,093,745 people employed out of an economically active population of 54,331,979[footnote 17].

1.3 Unemployment

1.3.1 The ESS EDHS 2024-5 June 2026 report noted that 55.8% of women and 14.5% of men in Tigray had not been employed during the 12 months preceding the survey[footnote 18]. Nationally, the corresponding figures were 50% for women and 8% for men[footnote 19].

1.3.2 The ESS NIHS September 2026 survey data indicated that Tigray accounted for approximately 5.7% of the country’s unemployed population (296,653 out of 5.24 million unemployed persons nationally) in 2024/25[footnote 20]. The data also showed that unemployment in Tigray was proportionately higher than the national average. Tigray’s unemployment rate stood at 12.0%, compared with 9.6% nationally. The data further indicated that Tigray had the third-highest unemployment rate among Ethiopia’s regions, behind Addis Ababa (19.1%) and Dire Dawa (14.5%), and above other large regions such as Oromia (10.5%)[footnote 21].

1.3.3 The same source noted that the female unemployment rate in Tigray was 12.5%, compared with 11.2% for males. Nationally, female unemployment was similar, at 12.8%, but male unemployment was lower, at 7.2%[footnote 22]. Youth unemployment in Tigray was 16.3%, compared with 12.9% nationally, the third-highest regional rate after Addis Ababa (20.3%) and Dire Dawa (17.7%). Oromia (14.4%) and Somali (13.1%) also recorded rates above the national average [footnote 23]. Unlike the national pattern, where female youth unemployment (17.4%) was almost twice the male rate (9.1%), youth unemployment in Tigray was broadly similar for young men (16.9%) and women (15.6%), with both rates exceeding the national average[footnote 24].

1.3.4 The ESS September 2026 report reported that unemployment was consistently higher in urban areas than in rural areas throughout Ethiopia. Nationally, urban unemployment stood at 17.2%, compared with 7.4% in rural areas. In Tigray, the urban-rural divide was particularly pronounced among young people. Youth unemployment in urban areas reached 23.0%, compared with 12.8% in rural areas, a gap of more than 10 percentage points. Tigray’s urban youth unemployment rate was also higher than the national urban average of 20.6%, while its rural youth unemployment rate exceeded the national rural average of 10.2%[footnote 25].
